opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there's something deeply right about it, and also something that's importantly incomplete. The right part is that the brain is fundamentally a prediction machine. We're constantly building models of the world, and we use the mismatch between what we expect and what actually happens to revise those models. That's very much in the spirit of the Bayesian picture of learning that a lot of us in developmental psychology have been working with for decades.

But here's the puzzle, and children make it really vivid. If you look at what babies and young kids actually do, they're not minimizing surprise at all. They're seeking it out. In our experiments, and in lots of others, when you show a baby something that violates their expectations, say a ball that seems to pass through a wall, they don't look away and settle back into a comfortable, predictable state. They look longer, and then they go and explore that very object. They'll bang it on the table to see if it's really solid. They'll drop it to see if it really floats. Kids are surprise-maximizers, at least in the short run.

Now, the Friston people have an answer to this. They say, well, you're minimizing expected surprise over the long run, so exploring now reduces surprise later. That's true as far as it goes, but I worry it becomes so flexible it stops telling you very much. If both seeking surprise and avoiding it count as minimizing surprise, the theory risks being unfalsifiable.

What I think is the more interesting way to frame it is in terms of the explore-exploit tradeoff. There's a real tension between exploiting what you already know to act effectively, and exploring to find out new things, even at the cost of being less effective right now. And my argument is that childhood is evolution's solution to that tension. You get this long, protected period where you're allowed to be a terrible exploiter, you can't feed yourself or do anything useful, but you're a tremendous explorer. And then as adults we shift toward exploiting. So minimizing surprise might be a pretty good description of what a middle-aged professor does most of the time, but it's not a very good description of what a four-year-old does. And I think the four-year-olds are actually the ones doing the most powerful learning.

r001.rationale: The response says the theory risks becoming unfalsifiable and may stop telling us much, but does not connect that concern to the difficulty of building an empirical research program.

r002.rationale: It says children seek out expectation-violating events, explore them, and use that exploration to learn.

r003.rationale: It explicitly worries that both seeking and avoiding surprise can count as minimizing it, making the theory too flexible and potentially unfalsifiable.

r004.rationale: The response does not connect Friston’s theory to the theory-theory framework; it mentions Bayesian learning and developmental psychology instead.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think Friston's picture captures something real, but I think it gets the children exactly backwards. If you look at what babies and young children actually do, they don't look like creatures who are trying to minimize surprise. They look like creatures who are seeking it out. A two-year-old will spend twenty minutes pouring water from one cup into another, or pushing the same button over and over, and what they're doing is systematically going to the places where their predictions are worst. The developmental data on this is quite robust now: children preferentially attend to events that violate their expectations, and then they explore those things more, and they learn more about them. That's the opposite of what you'd do if your goal were just to keep the world unsurprising.

Now, Friston would say, and this is the clever part of the free energy framework, that curiosity falls out of it anyway, because exploring now reduces your expected surprise later. Epistemic foraging, they call it. And formally that's fine. But at that point I think the theory has become so flexible that I'm not sure what it rules out. If staying in a dark room minimizes surprise and climbing on the bookshelf also minimizes surprise, then "minimizing surprise" isn't doing the explanatory work. Something else is, namely the trade-off between exploiting what you already know and exploring what you don't.

And that trade-off is really my whole story about childhood. The reason human beings have this absurdly long, helpless, expensive period of immaturity is that it lets you have one part of the life cycle devoted to exploration, where you're not responsible for getting dinner on the table, and then a later part devoted to exploitation. Children are the research and development department of the species. Adults are production and marketing. From that perspective, an adult brain does start to look a bit more Fristonian. We do get better at predicting and worse at noticing what we didn't predict. But I'd say that's the cost of being a grown-up, not the definition of learning.

r001.rationale: The response questions what the formalism rules out, but does not say it is difficult to connect to an empirical research program.

r002.rationale: It says children seek events where their predictions are worst, explore them, and learn more about them.

r003.rationale: It calls the theory so flexible that it is unclear what it rules out, directly expressing concern that it can accommodate many outcomes.

r004.rationale: The response discusses exploration of prediction violations but does not connect Friston’s theory to the theory-theory framework.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s an interesting framework, but the question is how much it actually explains. If you make the notion of minimizing surprise broad enough, you can describe almost anything an organism does in those terms. What’s harder is getting specific predictions about how learning works.

Children are a particularly interesting case because they seem to seek out surprise. They don’t just want to stay in a familiar environment where everything is predictable. They want to find the thing that doesn’t fit, poke it, and see what happens. That’s part of what makes them such effective learners.

Now, you can say that seeking surprise in the short run helps you reduce uncertainty in the long run. That’s a perfectly sensible idea. But then the explanatory work is in specifying when you explore, what you explore, and how you use what you discover. I’m more interested in those concrete questions than in whether we can put all of cognition under one very general principle.

r001.rationale: The response says the framework is harder to use for specific predictions about learning and that its explanatory value depends on concrete questions such as when and what organisms explore.

r002.rationale: It says children seek out surprises and investigate things that do not fit, presenting this as part of how they learn.

r003.rationale: It explicitly warns that defining surprise minimization broadly enough could describe almost anything an organism does.

r004.rationale: The response discusses Friston’s framework and children’s exploration, but it does not connect the theory to the theory-theory framework.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s something compelling about the idea that learning involves making predictions and revising them when they’re wrong. But I’m less convinced that minimizing surprise, by itself, explains what learners do. If that were your only aim, you could sit in a dark room and arrange never to encounter anything unexpected.

Children are especially interesting here because they actively seek out things that surprise them. They experiment. They do things just to find out what will happen. You can explain that within Friston’s framework by saying that they’re accepting surprise now to reduce uncertainty later. But then the question is whether the framework makes specific predictions about what they’ll explore and when they’ll stop.

So I think it’s a useful way of organizing some ideas. The challenge is getting from that very general principle to an explanation of the particular things children actually do.

r001.rationale: The response says the general principle must be turned into specific predictions about what children explore and when they stop, and calls that the challenge to explaining their particular behavior.

r002.rationale: It says children actively seek surprising things, experiment to find out what happens, and revise predictions when they are wrong.

r003.rationale: It calls the principle general, but does not clearly say the formalism can account for any outcome.

r004.rationale: It discusses children exploring surprising outcomes but does not connect this to the theory-theory framework.
